controls.statement: Maintain a complete API inventory.
Every API has an owner and documented consumers.
Interface schemas and behavior are versioned.
Authentication is enforced on every protected operation.
Authorization is evaluated for every object, property, operation, and tenant.
Input is validated against an explicit schema.
Unknown or prohibited fields are rejected or handled safely.
Content types and character encodings are constrained.
Request body, URL, header, nesting, field, query, and batch sizes are bounded.
Expensive queries and filters have cost controls.
Pagination has safe maximums.
Sorting and filtering cannot bypass access control.
Mass assignment and unexpected property binding are prevented.
HTTP methods have correct and consistent semantics.
Idempotency is implemented where retries can repeat effects.
Concurrency control prevents lost updates where required.
Timeouts exist for all outbound calls.
Retries are bounded and use backoff and jitter.
Retries occur only for safe or idempotent operations.
Circuit breaking or equivalent isolation exists for unstable dependencies.
Errors use consistent safe structures and appropriate status codes.
Error responses do not expose stack traces, queries, secrets, or internal topology.
Rate limits and quotas protect users, tenants, infrastructure, and dependencies.
Rate limits cannot be trivially bypassed through alternate identifiers or routes.
CORS uses explicit trusted origins where cross-origin access is needed.
Credentialed cross-origin requests do not use wildcard origins.
Browser-authenticated state-changing operations have CSRF protection.
Sensitive credentials and tokens never appear in URLs.
Redirects and callback destinations are strictly validated.
Server-side outbound destinations are constrained to prevent SSRF.
URL parsing is consistent across proxies, application code, and security controls.
Host-header and forwarded-header trust is explicitly configured.
Request smuggling, response splitting, cache poisoning, and parser ambiguity have been assessed.
Webhooks are authenticated or signed.
Webhooks include replay protection.
Webhook consumers are idempotent.
Webhook retries, ordering, failure, and reconciliation are defined.
API keys are scoped, rotated, revocable, and attributable.
Secrets are not returned in responses or documentation examples.
Backward compatibility is tested.
Breaking-change and deprecation policies exist.
Old versions have retirement dates and monitoring.
Contract tests cover external providers and consumers.
API documentation matches deployed behavior.
Production examples contain no real credentials or personal data.
Graph-based APIs limit depth, breadth, recursion, aliases, batching, and computational cost.
Graph schema introspection exposure is intentionally decided.
WebSocket or streaming connections authenticate securely.
Streaming connections verify origin where browser initiated.
Authorization changes and logout invalidate long-lived connections.
Reconnect, ordering, deduplication, backpressure, and heartbeat behavior are tested.
File-transfer APIs apply the file-security controls in this checklist.
Partner and machine-to-machine APIs use appropriately scoped identities.
Public APIs have abuse controls, usage policies, and security contact information.
Inventory every login, enrollment, recovery, federation, API, support, and administrative authentication path.
Select identity and authentication assurance appropriate to the harm of account compromise.
Require stronger authentication for privileged and high-impact accounts.
Support phishing-resistant authentication where risk warrants it.
Multifactor enrollment is protected from account takeover.
New authenticators require appropriate reauthentication.
Removing or replacing an authenticator requires appropriate verification.
Password handling follows current guidance.
Passwords are not silently truncated or transformed unexpectedly.
Common and compromised passwords are rejected where password authentication is used.
Password managers and paste are supported.
Login defenses address credential stuffing and brute force.
Defenses avoid creating trivial denial-of-service against legitimate users.
Login, registration, and recovery responses do not unnecessarily disclose whether an account exists.
Account enrollment verifies the correct communication channel or identity evidence.
Account recovery is no weaker than normal authentication.
Recovery cannot be redirected through an unverified channel.
Recovery tokens are single-use, short-lived, random, and stored safely.
Password or authenticator reset invalidates appropriate sessions and recovery material.
High-risk operations require recent authentication.
Email, phone, payout, identity, and security-setting changes notify the user appropriately.
Changes to recovery information use delayed or additional verification where warranted.
Default credentials are absent.
Test, dormant, abandoned, and terminated accounts are disabled.
Service accounts cannot use interactive recovery mechanisms inappropriately.
Authentication events are audited.
Suspicious authentication can trigger step-up controls or investigation.
Users can review and revoke relevant sessions and devices.
Clock skew and token timing behavior are tested.
Recovery codes are protected, single-use, and regenerated securely.
Support personnel cannot bypass identity checks without a controlled, audited exception process.
Social-engineering resistance is included in support procedures.
Issuer, audience, signature, algorithm, expiration, nonce, and state are validated.
Redirect URIs are matched exactly according to the protocol’s security requirements.
Authorization-code flows use current protections such as proof-key mechanisms where applicable.
Deprecated or insecure delegated-authorization flows are not used.
Token substitution and mix-up attacks are addressed.
Identity-provider accounts are linked only after secure verification.
Automatic account linking cannot merge an attacker’s identity with a victim’s account.
Tokens are scoped to the minimum required audience and permissions.
Access and refresh tokens are stored and transmitted safely.
Refresh-token rotation and reuse detection are applied where appropriate.
Revocation, logout, key rotation, and identity-provider outage behavior are tested.
Federation metadata and signing keys are refreshed safely.
Identity claims are not trusted beyond their documented assurance.
Tenant or organization selection cannot be manipulated to cross boundaries.
Authorization is denied by default.
Authorization is enforced server-side at every trusted boundary.
A current role-permission-resource matrix exists.
Every endpoint and action maps to a required permission.
Access checks use the current user, tenant, resource, and operation.
Object ownership is verified on every direct and indirect object reference.
Horizontal privilege escalation has been tested.
Vertical privilege escalation has been tested.
Function-level and property-level authorization have been tested.
Bulk, export, search, reporting, and aggregation endpoints enforce the same controls as individual records.
Hidden fields and client-side controls cannot grant access.
Role changes take effect promptly across sessions, caches, queues, and services.
Removed users lose access to shared resources.
Nested groups and inherited permissions are tested.
Temporary permissions expire automatically.
Privileged access follows least privilege and just-in-time principles where practical.
High-impact actions require additional approval where appropriate.
Administrative, support, and impersonation actions require reason, authorization, visible indication, and audit.
Impersonation never exposes secrets the support user should not receive.
Emergency access is time-bounded and reviewed.
Authorization decisions are logged at an appropriate level.
Background jobs retain correct authorization and tenant context.
Caches do not return data authorized for another principal.
Search indexes preserve authorization boundaries.
Files, exports, backups, logs, and analytics preserve tenant boundaries.
Queue messages cannot be reassigned across tenants through manipulated metadata.
Tenant-specific encryption, keys, domains, and configuration are isolated as designed.
Resource identifiers alone are never treated as authorization.
Side channels do not disclose another tenant’s existence, activity, identifiers, or resource usage.
Automated tests cover every role × operation × resource-state combination considered material.
Session identifiers have sufficient unpredictability.
Session identifiers are generated using a cryptographically secure source.
Session identifiers are never accepted from insecure or unintended channels.
Browser cookies use `Secure` where transmitted over HTTPS.
Sensitive browser cookies use `HttpOnly` unless script access is essential and justified.
`SameSite` behavior is intentionally selected and tested.
Cookie domain and path scope are as narrow as practical.
Cross-subdomain cookie trust is explicitly assessed.
Session identifiers rotate after login and privilege changes.
Session fixation is prevented.
Idle and absolute timeouts match risk and user needs.
Logout invalidates the server-side session or otherwise revokes access.
Account recovery and credential change invalidate appropriate sessions.
Concurrent-session policy is defined.
Users can identify and revoke sessions where appropriate.
“Remember me” behavior has separate, appropriately constrained credentials.
Sensitive state-changing actions have CSRF protection.
Tokens validate issuer, audience, subject, type, signature, algorithm, expiry, and not-before values.
A token intended for one purpose cannot be accepted for another.
Token replay risk is addressed.
Refresh credentials are rotated or otherwise protected against replay where appropriate.
Tokens and session identifiers are absent from URLs, referrers, analytics, logs, and error reports.
Client-side storage of tokens is minimized and threat-modeled.
Logout, revocation, and compromise behavior is tested across all application components.
Session-related logs do not expose reusable credentials.
All untrusted input is identified.
